topics.title: Stack vs Heap Lifetime & Ownership Semantics
topics.description: Understanding memory allocation mechanics, cache locality, and deterministic stack lifetimes.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Stack Memory is fast, automatic, LIFO memory managed by CPU stack pointer adjustments. Heap Memory is dynamic memory allocated via new / malloc requiring explicit lifetime management.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Stack allocation is nanoseconds fast ($O(1)$ stack pointer move) with perfect CPU cache locality. Heap allocation involves operating system free-list searches ($O(N)$ allocator overhead) and pointer indirection.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Default to stack allocation. Use heap allocation only when objects must outlive the current scope, have dynamic sizes, or require polymorphic base pointers.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Stack objects are destroyed automatically when exiting scope. Heap objects must be wrapped in RAII smart pointers.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Real-time game loops, high-performance packet parsers, database engines.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Prefer stack objects for value semantics. Use heap for polymorphism and dynamic buffers.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not allocate huge 50MB buffers on the stack (triggers Stack Overflow crash).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Stack gives deterministic cleanup and maximum CPU cache efficiency.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Stack size is strictly limited per thread.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Stack, Heap, Static/BSS segment, Thread-Local Storage (TLS).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Returning a pointer to a stack-allocated local variable.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What causes a Stack Overflow error in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Allocating an array too large for the stack (e.g. int arr[10000000];) or infinite deep recursion without a base exit condition.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement a fixed-size StackArena allocator.

referenceCode.code: class StackArena { char buf[1024]; int offset{0}; public: void* alloc(size_t s) { void* p = &buf[offset]; offset += s; return p; } };

sections.content: Mastering Stack vs Heap Lifetime & Ownership Semantics is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: Smart Pointer Ownership Models & Custom Deleters
topics.description: Deep dive into std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr control blocks, and integrating C API custom deleters.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Smart pointers express explicit ownership semantics in modern C++: exclusive (unique_ptr), shared (shared_ptr), and observing (weak_ptr).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Eliminates memory leaks, dangling pointers, and double-free vulnerabilities.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Custom deleters allow smart pointers to manage non-memory OS handles (e.g. C file handles, sockets, database transaction handles).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: std::unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> file(fopen("..."), &fclose);.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

sections.content: UniqueSocket wraps MockSocket with custom closeMockSocket deleter.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: C API integrations (OpenSSL SSL_free, POSIX close, SDL_DestroyWindow).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use custom deleters whenever wrapping legacy C handles in RAII.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not pass stateful heavy custom deleters to unique_ptr without considering type bloat.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Automatic leak-free management of any C handle.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: unique_ptr type includes the deleter signature.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Function pointer deleters, Lambda deleters, Functor deleters.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Creating two independent shared_ptr instances from the same raw pointer.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is the custom deleter of std::shared_ptr not part of its type?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Because std::shared_ptr uses Type Erasure in its heap control block to store the deleter, keeping the std::shared_ptr<T> type clean and uniform.

sections.content: Create unique_ptr wrapper calling glDeleteTextures custom deleter.

topics.title: Circular Dependency Resolution with std::weak_ptr
topics.description: Breaking cyclic shared_ptr memory leaks using non-owning weak references.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A Circular Reference occurs when Object A holds a std::shared_ptr to Object B, and Object B holds a std::shared_ptr to Object A, causing reference counts to stay $\ge 1$ forever (Memory Leak).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Even though all external pointers go out of scope, the objects keep each other alive in memory indefinitely.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Break the cycle: Child holds std::weak_ptr<Parent> back-pointer.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: weak_ptr increments weak_count, NOT use_count. To use it, call wp.lock() returning a temporary shared_ptr.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Weak Pointer Lock
callout.text: std::shared_ptr<Parent> p = child->parent.lock(); if (p) { p->doSomething(); } // Safe access!

sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Button uses std::weak_ptr preventing circular reference memory leaks.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: DOM Trees, Observer subscriber registries, Graph structures, Cache expiry observers.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use weak_ptr for parent back-pointers, caches, and observer registries.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use weak_ptr if the relationship is exclusive ownership (use unique_ptr).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Completely eliminates reference cycle memory leaks.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires calling lock() before accessing the underlying object.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: std::weak_ptr, std::enable_shared_from_this.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Dereferencing a weak_ptr directly without checking if lock() returned non-null.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does std::enable_shared_from_this use weak_ptr internally?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: It holds a private std::weak_ptr<T> to this. Calling shared_from_this() locks this internal weak pointer, safely returning a new std::shared_ptr<T> without creating a duplicate control block.
